rationale.intervention_reconstruction: The hypothesis proposes high-temperature mechanical tests under simulated plasma-facing conditions, while the paper actually performed room-temperature compression, temperature-dependent indentation plastometry up to 500 °C, and room-temperature scratch testing. Both involve mechanical testing of the same alloy versus pure tungsten, but the specific test methods and temperature ranges differ substantially.
rationale.condition_agreement: The hypothesis specifies temperatures of 1200–1500 K and controlled atmospheres to mimic irradiation, whereas the paper used room temperature to 500 °C in air for indentation and room temperature for compression and scratch tests. These are different temperature regimes and environments.
rationale.mechanism_agreement: The hypothesis attributes improved plasticity and toughness to Zr segregation at grain boundaries enhancing cohesion. The paper attributes improvements to Ti, V, and Zr through reduced valence-electron concentration, dislocation-core modification, grain-boundary cohesion, and impeded crack propagation, but does not isolate grain-boundary segregation as the primary mechanism. Both invoke grain-boundary cohesion, but the specific pathway (segregation vs. multicomponent effects) differs.
rationale.outcome_agreement: The hypothesis predicts higher plastic strain and toughness at high temperatures with Zr enrichment at grain boundaries. The paper reports higher strength, greater plastic strain, lower brittle-to-ductile transition, less scratch damage, and higher fracture toughness, but at lower temperatures and without measuring grain-boundary segregation. The predicted property and direction match, but the specifics of temperature and microstructural evidence differ.
